titulo: Town, places and directions: Asking for and giving directions

aula.objetivo: Name places in town, say where they are with «vicino a», «davanti a» and similar expressions, ask for and give directions with the formal imperative, and choose a means of transport. Avoid the English-speaker traps: leaving out «a» after «vicino», using one imperative for everyone, and «by bus» with «per».

blocos.titulo: Giving directions with the formal imperative
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: to attract someone's attention, say «Scusi» (formal) or «Scusa» (informal). English «excuse me» works for everyone. STEP 2: the useful question is «Scusi, per andare in centro?» (Excuse me, how do I get to the center?). STEP 3: the answer uses the formal «Lei» imperative: «Vada dritto» (go straight), «Giri a destra» (turn right), «Giri a sinistra» (turn left), «Attraversi la piazza» (cross the square), «Prenda la prima a destra» (take the first on the right). STEP 4: among friends, the informal imperative («tu») is used: «Vai dritto», «Gira a destra», «Prendi la seconda a sinistra». STEP 5: to say where to stop: «È in fondo alla strada», «È dopo il semaforo», «È prima dell'incrocio». STEP 6: pronunciation: «destra» is «DEHS-trah» and «sinistra» is «see-NEE-strah». «Dritto» and «diritto» are two spellings of the same word. STEP 7: the usual way to say «to the right» and «to the left» is «a destra» and «a sinistra», with «a» and no article. STEP 8: after «fino a», use the merged form: «fino al semaforo», «fino alla piazza».
blocos.comparacao: English gives directions with a single form for everyone: «Turn left». Italian chooses between a formal and an informal imperative, depending on who you are speaking to: «Giri a sinistra» to a stranger, «Gira a sinistra» to a friend. The formal form looks like the third person («giri», «vada»), which is the form of «Lei». If you remember one rule, make it that.

Explain aloud why English «Turn left» has two Italian versions.
